passages.happening: Early in the morning the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole council make their plan. They tie Jesus up and hand him over to Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate asks him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus answers, “You have said so.” The chief priests accuse him of many things. Pilate asks why he does not answer. Jesus says nothing more, and Pilate is amazed.
passages.hearers:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. In 1961 Italian archaeologists working at Caesarea, the Roman capital on the coast, found a stone with his name on it. It calls him ‘prefect of Judea’. It is the only inscription that scholars all agree names him. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around AD 116, says that Christ was executed in the reign of Tiberius by Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44).

The Jewish writers Josephus and Philo, who lived in that century, describe Pilate as harsh. Josephus tells how he brought army standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem by night, against Jewish law, and withdrew them only after a great protest. Philo accuses him of greed, violence, and theft. Their accounts are hostile, but they show a governor who was not easily pushed around.

Notice how the question has changed. Before the council the issue was whether Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One. Before Pilate it is whether he is ‘King of the Jews’. To Rome, a man claiming to be a king was a rebel against Caesar. That was a charge a Roman governor would take seriously.
passages.ot: Jesus' silence again recalls Isaiah's servant, who “did not open His mouth” though “oppressed and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:7).
passages.hard: Why does Pilate decide the case, and not the council? John's Gospel says the council told Pilate they had no right to put anyone to death (John 18:31). Historians discuss how strict that limit was, since Jewish authorities did sometimes carry out killings, such as the stoning of Stephen in Acts 7. But crucifixion was a Roman punishment, carried out under a Roman governor's authority. Whatever the council decided in the night, the sentence of death on the cross was Pilate's.
passages.asks: Jesus says very little before Pilate. He does not plead or argue. Ask what it means that the King of all things stood silent in a governor's court. There is a strength in not needing to win every argument. There is also a cost in telling the truth to power, and Jesus paid it.

passages.happening: At the feast it was Pilate's custom to release one prisoner the people asked for. A man named Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. A crowd comes and asks Pilate to keep his custom. Pilate offers them ‘the King of the Jews’, because he knows the chief priests handed Jesus over out of envy. But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. Pilate asks what he should do with Jesus. They shout, “Crucify Him!” Pilate asks, “What evil has He done?” They shout louder. Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands him over to be crucified.
passages.hearers:
Rebels against Rome were common in those years, and an ‘insurrection’ means an uprising. Barabbas was the kind of man Rome usually crucified.

Flogging was a Roman whipping, often given before crucifixion. It was brutal, and it left a person very weak.

The name Barabbas is Aramaic and means ‘son of the father’. Mark does not make anything of this, but many readers have noticed the irony: one ‘son of the father’ goes free, and the true Son of the Father dies in his place.
passages.ot: Isaiah's servant was “numbered with the transgressors” and “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). A guilty man walks free and an innocent one is condemned. Christians have long seen in Barabbas a picture of every person for whom Jesus died.
passages.hard:
Was there really a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover? No record of it has been found outside the Gospels. Some scholars think the scene was shaped by the early church to make a point. Others note that Roman rulers did sometimes grant pardons at festivals elsewhere, and think a local custom in Judea is quite possible. These notes leave the question open.

This passage has also been misused, terribly. For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. Mark tells of a particular crowd in one city on one morning, stirred up by particular leaders, and of a Roman governor who gave the order and Roman soldiers who carried it out. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews. In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).
passages.asks: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and condemned him anyway, to keep a crowd quiet. Ask where you are tempted to do what is easy rather than what is right because of pressure from others. And ask whether you see yourself in Barabbas: someone set free by the death of another.

passages.happening: The soldiers take Jesus into the governor's headquarters and call the whole company together. They dress him in purple, twist a crown out of thorns, and put it on his head. They salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” They hit him on the head with a staff, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. Then they take off the purple, put his own clothes back on him, and lead him out to crucify him.
passages.hearers:
The soldiers are acting out a coronation as a cruel joke. Purple was the color of kings and emperors. A crown, a salute, and kneeling were how people honored a ruler.

Mark explains the place with the Latin word praetorium, the governor's headquarters, one of several Latin words in his Gospel.

The great irony is that every part of the joke is true. The man in the purple cloak really is the king. The mockers do not know that their mock worship is aimed at the one who deserves real worship.
passages.ot: Isaiah's servant says, “I offered My back to those who struck Me,” and “I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6). Jesus himself had said in 10:34 that the Gentiles would mock him, spit on him, flog him, and kill him.
passages.hard: Why does Mark describe the mocking in such detail, but say almost nothing of the pain of crucifixion? Mark seems more interested in what the scene means than in how it felt. He shows the world's view of Jesus as a fake king, so that the reader can see the truth underneath. It is wise to follow Mark here and not to linger on the cruelty for its own sake.
passages.asks: The soldiers knelt to Jesus as a joke. Ask whether there are ways you give Jesus the outward signs of honor without meaning them. Jesus let himself be made a fool of by men he could have destroyed. That is what his kind of kingship looks like.

passages.happening: The soldiers force a man passing by, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry Jesus' cross. They bring Jesus to Golgotha, which means ‘the place of the skull’. They offer him wine mixed with myrrh, but he does not take it. They crucify him and gamble for his clothes. It is the third hour, about nine in the morning. The notice of the charge reads THE KING OF THE JEWS. Two robbers are crucified with him, one on each side. People passing by shake their heads and jeer. The chief priests and scribes mock him too: “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!” Even the men crucified with him insult him.
passages.hearers:
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and violent criminals. It was meant to be slow, public, and shameful, a warning to everyone who passed. The Roman writer Cicero called it the cruelest and most disgusting penalty. Josephus says that during the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, Roman soldiers crucified as many as five hundred captured Jews a day outside the walls (Jewish War 5.449-451).

Archaeology adds one direct witness. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in north Jerusalem, builders found a stone box of bones for a man named Yehohanan. His right heel bone still had an iron nail through it, with bits of wood attached. Later study corrected some early details, but the find shows plainly that victims were nailed, and that at least one crucified Jewish man was buried in his family's tomb. Remains like this are very rare.

Mark tells none of the physical details. He simply writes, “And they crucified Him.” His first hearers knew what that meant.

Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Roman soldiers could force a civilian to carry a load. Mark names Simon's sons as if his readers knew them. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome (Romans 16:13). Some think he was the same man, but the name was common, and no one can be sure.

Jewish and Roman hours were counted from sunrise. The third hour was about nine in the morning, the sixth about noon, and the ninth about three in the afternoon.
passages.ot:
Psalm 22 runs all through this scene. “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing” (Psalm 22:18). “All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads” (Psalm 22:7).

Some manuscripts add a verse 28 that quotes Isaiah 53:12, “He was numbered with the transgressors.” The oldest manuscripts do not have it, which is why many Bibles skip from verse 27 to 29. Luke records Jesus applying those words to himself (Luke 22:37).
passages.hard:
The mockers say, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!” They mean it as an insult. Mark means it as the truth. Jesus had said that whoever wants to save his life will lose it (8:35), and that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). He does not come down from the cross, not because he cannot, but because staying there is how he saves others.

The wine mixed with myrrh may have been offered to dull the pain. Jesus refuses it. Mark does not explain why. Many think he chose to face what was coming with a clear mind.
passages.asks: Simon was a stranger passing by, and he ended up carrying the cross of Jesus. Mark names his sons, which suggests the family later became known among the Christians. Ask what crosses have been put on your shoulders that you did not choose, and whether they might also bring you nearer to Jesus. And notice who is mocking: the passersby, the leaders, and even the dying men next to him. Mark leaves no group outside.

passages.t: Darkness, the cry, and the torn curtain
passages.happening: At noon darkness covers the whole land until three in the afternoon. At three Jesus cries out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” Some standing near think he is calling Elijah. Someone soaks a sponge in sour wine and holds it up to him, saying, “Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down.” Jesus gives a loud cry and breathes his last. The curtain of the temple is torn in two from top to bottom. The Roman centurion standing in front of him sees how he died and says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
passages.hearers:
Mark keeps Jesus' words in Aramaic, the language he spoke at home. The bystanders hear ‘Eloi’ and think of Elijah. Many Jews believed Elijah would come again before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and some pictured him coming to help the righteous in trouble.

Sour wine was a cheap, vinegary drink that soldiers and laborers drank.

The temple had curtains that separated the holy places. The inner one hung before the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went, once a year. A large outer one hung at the entrance to the sanctuary.

A centurion was a Roman officer who commanded a company of soldiers. Mark places this one right in front of the cross. He is the first human being in Mark's story to call Jesus the Son of God, and he says it while looking at a dead man on a cross.
passages.ot:
Jesus' cry is the first line of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” The psalm begins in the depths, but it does not end there. It turns to trust: “He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help” (Psalm 22:24). It ends with the nations turning to God: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD” (Psalm 22:27).

The darkness recalls Amos: “I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime” (Amos 8:9).

The sour wine recalls Psalm 69:21: “They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.”
passages.hard:
Was Jesus truly abandoned by God? Christians have read the cry in several ways.

Some stress that Jesus is praying a psalm. A psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind, and Psalm 22 ends in trust and victory. So the cry is faith spoken from the depths, not despair.

Others insist that the first line must be heard in its full force. Jesus felt real abandonment and did not pretend otherwise. Many connect this with Paul's words that God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 5:21): Jesus bore the judgment due to sin, including the loss of the felt presence of God.

Others say that Jesus spoke for the whole human race he had joined, voicing our forsakenness as his own.

These readings can overlap, and Christians who share the faith of the creeds hold them in different blends. Even in the cry, Jesus still calls God ‘my God’. These notes do not settle how best to describe what the Son went through.

Why was the curtain torn? Some read it as a sign that the way into God's presence is now open, as the letter to the Hebrews says, “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20). Others read it as a sign of judgment on the temple, which Jesus had said would fall (13:2). Many hold both. Scholars also differ on whether Mark means the inner or the outer curtain. Notice that Mark uses the same Greek word for ‘torn’ only once before, when the heavens are ‘torn open’ at Jesus' baptism (1:10).

The cry also speaks to anyone who has felt forsaken by God. Jesus did not hide that feeling. He took it to God in the words of Scripture. If you feel that way, you can pray it too, and you should not stay alone with it. Tell someone you trust, and if you are in danger, reach out for help today.
passages.asks: The centurion believed by watching how Jesus died. Not by a miracle, but by the cross. Ask what you see when you look at the cross: weakness and failure, or the place where God is most clearly shown. And if you have ever prayed ‘why have You forsaken me?’, notice that Jesus prayed it first.

passages.t: The women watching, and the burial
passages.happening: Women are watching from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, and Salome. They had followed Jesus in Galilee and cared for his needs, and many other women had come up to Jerusalem with him. Evening comes. It is the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath. Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was waiting for the kingdom of God, goes boldly to Pilate and asks for the body. Pilate is surprised Jesus is already dead and checks with the centurion. Then he gives the body to Joseph. Joseph buys a linen cloth, takes the body down, wraps it, and lays it in a tomb cut out of the rock. He rolls a stone against the entrance. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses see where he is laid.
passages.hearers:
The men have run away. The women stay. Mark has hardly mentioned them before, and now he tells us they had followed Jesus all along. They watch the death, they see the burial, and in the next chapter they will be the first to find the tomb empty. Mark is careful to say that they saw where the body was laid. They did not go to the wrong tomb.

The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday. The law of Moses said the body of an executed man must not be left hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23). So the burial had to be done quickly, before dark.

It took courage for Joseph to go to Pilate. He was a member of the very council that had condemned Jesus, and asking for the body of a man executed for treason meant openly siding with him.

Wealthier families cut tombs into the rock outside the city. A body was laid inside, and the entrance was closed with a large stone.
passages.ot:
The law said, “you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Joseph keeps that law for Jesus.

Isaiah's servant “was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death” (Isaiah 53:9).
passages.hard:
Did Jesus really die, or did he only faint? Mark takes care to answer this. The centurion who oversaw the execution confirms to Pilate that Jesus is dead. Joseph wraps the body and closes the tomb. The women see it. In Mark's account there is no doubt: Jesus was dead and buried.

Another question is the council. Mark says the whole council condemned Jesus (14:64). Yet here a member of the council honors him. Luke says Joseph had not agreed with their decision (Luke 23:51). Mark shows that not even the council was all of one mind.
passages.asks: The women could do nothing to stop what happened. They could only stay and watch. Sometimes faithfulness looks like that: staying near when everyone else has gone. Joseph, on the other hand, finally stepped out of hiding. Ask whether you are more like the disciples who ran, the women who stayed, or Joseph, who waited a long time before he was brave.
